quotes.note: Sustained external narration refers to Charlotte as “she” while reporting her perceptions and pain; this is third-person internal focalization.
A character’s direct speech, including the quoted first-person declaration, does not expose the base narrator.
Direct speech addressed to Charlotte; its first- and second-person pronouns belong to the speaker.
Sustained narration presents Charlotte externally as “she” while rendering her questions and feelings through third-person focalization.
A single narratorial sentence about “they” is compatible with third-person narration but is too context-poor to establish the controlling narrator by itself.
The passage is chiefly Laurie’s direct speech; the short third-person speech beats are insufficient to diagnose the base narrator independently.
A sustained scene narrates Hoyt and Charlotte externally and gives access to Charlotte’s sensations and question without making the narrator a participant.
Clipped direct dialogue whose “we,” “you,” and “I” belong to speaking characters, not the base narrator.
The fragment is too severely clipped to recover its quotation boundaries or narratorial context.
Sustained external scene narration repeatedly identifies Charlotte as “she” and Hoyt as “he,” with no participating narrator.
The narrator externally calls Charlotte “she” while reporting her prior thoughts and present perception, establishing third-person internal focalization.

web_evidence.title: I Am Charlotte Simmons
web_evidence.note: The publisher-authorized prologue is sustained third-person narration centered on Hoyt, including external reference to him and access to his thoughts.

web_evidence.title: The Return of Omniscience in Contemporary Fiction
web_evidence.note: Paul Dawson’s scholarly narratological analysis treats the novel’s controlling voice as an omniscient, heterodiegetic narrator and describes its ethnographic distance and explanatory commentary throughout the book.

web_evidence.title: You Know What? Tom Wolfe Book Is Lots Of Fun
web_evidence.note: The review explicitly identifies a close third-person point of view that shifts among characters across the novel.

web_evidence.title: An Unsentimental Education
web_evidence.note: Merve Emre analyzes Wolfe’s free-indirect method as rendering characters’ first-person thoughts within third-person narration and discusses its use for Charlotte and several other characters across the novel.

web_evidence.title: A-level English Literature A Examiner Report, Paper 2B, June 2017
web_evidence.note: The examiner report explicitly distinguishes Wolfe’s third-person narrative stance from the focalization of an arrival-at-university extract through Charlotte.

search_log: Searched “I Am Charlotte Simmons Tom Wolfe excerpt first chapter” and opened Macmillan’s authorized prologue; Google Books supplied bibliographic and contents data but no additional diagnostic prose was used.

Searched the title with “third person,” “point of view,” “narrator,” and “close third-person”; opened the Observer review and AQA examiner report, both of which explicitly identify third-person narration.

Searched scholarly sources on narration and focalization; located Paul Dawson’s Narrative article analyzing the novel’s omniscient heterodiegetic narrator throughout the book. The CiteSeer PDF timed out on a subsequent open attempt, but its indexed article text and publication metadata were available in the live search results.

Searched for alternating narrators, multiple narrators, first-person narration, second-person narration, epistolary form, and frame narrative; found no evidence of sustained base sections in another person. BookRags assertions and Goodreads review prose were treated as lower-value corroboration and omitted from the evidence list.

Opened the New York Review of Books essay, which explains that apparent first-person thought is free indirect discourse embedded in third-person narration and traces that technique across multiple characters.
person_note: The quote set repeatedly shows a nonparticipating narrator rendering Charlotte’s actions, sensations, and thoughts in third person. Web evidence independently identifies the same structure: an omniscient or close-third narrator whose focalization shifts among Charlotte, Hoyt, and other characters. First-person forms such as “I am Charlotte Simmons” are character speech, thought, or a recurring mantra, while conversational or generic “you” is not sustained second-person protagonist narration. The authorized excerpt covers only the opening, but whole-book scholarly and critical analyses resolve that scope limitation; no credible evidence of alternating base-person sections was found.
